item.title: AI Finds its Way Into Backcountry Search and Rescue
item.dc:creator: Karen Emslie
item.description: AI is transforming how search and rescue is carried out, and also enabling rescuers to build bespoke solutions for their teams.
item.content:encoded:
Encountering a drone during a revitalizing mountain hike can feel irksome and intrusive unless you are lost or injured; then, it just might save your life. Drone technologies and AI are increasingly vital components of search and rescue (SAR) assignments. In some cases, SAR efforts that previously took days can be reduced to hours. AI is not only transforming how SAR is carried out, but it is also enabling rescuers to build bespoke solutions for their teams.

A New Team Member

Think Colorado, think wilderness. The 103,717.5 sq. mi. state abounds with mountains, canyons, ravines, rivers, and forests; it has an average altitude of 6,800 ft., rising to a peak of 14,433 ft. at Mount Elbert. It is an outdoor enthusiast’s paradise. According to a report by market research firm Longwoods International, Colorado received 96.8 million visitors in 2025. In summer, millions of people safely enjoy activities like hiking, climbing, and whitewater rafting, but inevitably, some get lost or injured. Each year, the Colorado Search and Rescue Association (CSAR) responds to around 3,000 SAR incidents, which can also include urban SAR when, for example, a child or an Alzheimer’s patient becomes lost.

CSAR is an umbrella organization that coordinates volunteer SAR networks in the state, including Boulder Emergency Squad (BES), Rocky Mountain Rescue, and Front Range Rescue Dogs. Steve Lanaghen is a long-serving rescuer with the special tactics group of BES: “We’re a very multifaceted group,” he said. “We do water rescue, dive rescue, airplane crashes, backcountry search, urban search, law support, fire support.”

Lanaghen has witnessed how technology has changed SAR over the decades. “We’ve gone from using pencils and paper maps on the hood of a car to figure out where people are, to now having a mobile command center with multiple monitors and Starlink; we can stream video back into our emergency operations center in the city.”

BES has been using drones since 2013. They transformed SAR by enabling what Lanaghen called “a bird’s eye view” of a search area, while reducing risk by providing overwatch for rescuers in hazardous conditions, like steep vertical work or river rescues. Today, the squad’s fleet of drones is augmented by AI technologies like computer vision for anomaly detection and thermal imaging, which uses temperature variation to spot missing people in visually obscured areas, like forests.

Mike Kabjian, who works alongside Lanaghen at BES, sees AI as “a search team member that can do things we can’t.” Models can now analyze drone footage pixel-by-pixel in real time and identify subtle color, shape, or motion anomalies that could signal the location of a person. Kabjian pointed to software such as Eagle Eyes, which “draws a little circle on the screen when it sees a color that statistically shouldn’t be there,” he said. “We’re looking for a person, but it could also be a jacket, a shoe, a backpack.”

The squad also can analyze data from drone live streams, georeferenced aerials maps, and thermal imagery via tools like Nova Maps and ADIAT, and are working with a Boulder-based technology startup, Odin Autonomy, to automate and streamline the operation of swarms of drones on SAR missions.

Lanaghen sees no tension between technology and the outdoors. “We have a lot of people who are very comfortable in the woods and very comfortable behind a computer.” He keeps a keen eye on how the latest AI advances could improve SAR, flagging robotic olfaction or e-nose systems as “out there” but full of potential. Lanaghen said future SAR AI systems could be made up of multiple sensors working together: “Some super-mobile sensor that can fly, swim, crawl under rocks or whatever; that can sense all these different things. It’ll give us a completely different view of what’s out there.”

On a planet full of wilderness, it is unsurprising for AI SAR to have global reach. In June, Fire and Rescue New South Wales in Australia found two missing hikers in Kosciuszko National Park within five hours using an AI-powered drone. Meanwhile, Salvamont, Romania’s National Mountain Rescuers Association, has partnered with Vodafone to build an AI-powered SAR system that captures and analyzes geolocated images to find missing hikers and climbers. In research, a team from Glasgow University, Scotland, has developed a deep reinforcement learning model for optimizing drones’ search paths, and an Italian team has presented an automated object detection pipeline for finding people lost in forests using real-time thermal video.

The SAR Programmer

It is not only developers and researchers who are innovating AI for SAR. For Kabjian, one of the greatest impacts of AI on SAR is enabling non-technical rescuers to build solutions. Tools for de-confliction, that is, knowing the position of other drones in an area to avoid accidents, exist, but can be expensive or not an exact fit for a SAR team’s needs, so Kabjian built his own. Using AI as a programming assistant, he created a drone finder that plots positional data onto CalTopo, the backcountry map software the squad uses. Design of the hardware—external antenna on the command vehicle—also was assisted by AI. As Kabjian puts it, “AI’s not in the product, but AI built the product.”

It is an approach he and Lanaghen currently are deploying to design an SAR video streaming system that fits the squad’s specific technical and privacy needs. “We need it fed without any lag into our command vehicle,” said Kabjian. “Simultaneous to that, we need an encrypted stream going to the cloud, not using RTSP [Real-Time Streaming Protocol], but using SRT [Secure Reliable Transport].”

Another area ripe for improvement with AI is SAR management. Kabjian described “the madness that is the first hour of a search,” when information like a person’s description and where they might have gone need to be processed and rescuers are mustering. “There’s people talking to you, there’s trucks coming, and everybody’s excited to go do something. It’s cognitive overload,” he said. Kabjian and Lanaghen aim to make this process “a more efficient machine” by automating rescuer check-in and form filling, and using AI to carry out initial planning and suggest rescue assignments.

Despite enthusiastically embracing AI, both seasoned rescuers stressed they will always take a strict “human-in-the-loop” verification approach. Said Kabjian, “Our key focus is life safety, we won’t be able to turn that completely over to a computer. We need experienced rescuers’ eyes on it to make sure that no one is endangered by the technology’s decision-making.”

For many, time in the wilderness means a break from technology, but when it comes to search and rescue, an AI-loaded drone whirring overhead will likely to be very welcome.

Karen Emslie is a location-independent freelance journalist and essayist.

item.title: Benchmarks for Data Agents
item.dc:creator: Abhilash Rao Mesala
item.description: The code world has benchmarks for questions about which LLM-based agent works better. We need something similar for data agents.
item.content:encoded:
Recently I had to figure out which of two agents was better at the work my team actually does. I mean LLM-based agents that write and change data pipelines: the SQL transformations, the schema changes that reshape a table’s columns and types, the backfills. I wanted a number, some way to say this one is worth more than that one. What I had instead was a hunch that one seemed better. The code world has benchmarks for exactly this kind of question. The data world does not.

Satish Chandra made this case for coding agents in a recent BLOG@CACM post. He laid out five things a good benchmark suite needs: representativeness (the tasks look like real work); headroom (scores still have room to climb); freedom from contamination (the answers haven’t leaked into the model’s training data); a low cost to run; and scorability (a clear way to mark an answer right or wrong). Every one of them is harder for data than for code. Three of them are where data work hurts most: scorability, representativeness, and cost. I’ll start there and come back to the other two.

Take scorability first. A code benchmark grades against hidden tests: the patch either makes them pass or it doesn’t. Data work has no equivalent test to hide. The correct answer to a schema change is rarely a single value; it’s a shape. Row counts in a plausible range, a null rate that didn’t suddenly jump, a revenue number that didn’t move when nobody asked it to. Which shape counts as correct depends on what the dashboards, models, and downstream pipelines reading that table expected it to mean.

Representativeness doesn’t survive either, because data tasks won’t hold still. I do have a script that scores one task against a frozen snapshot of data. It’s useful for about three weeks. After that a schema has moved, an upstream source has quietly changed what a field means, and the snapshot no longer looks like anything running in production.

And cost. Cost is the one that scares me. Each data task drags a whole environment behind it: an upstream source, the warehouse where the data lands, the monitoring and tooling wrapped around it, and a set of downstream consumers whose expectations are what “correct” even means. Standing that up once is expensive. Standing it up for a thousand tasks, over and over, is a different order of problem.

So what can we do?

Score Meaning, Not Execution

A code solution is graded on whether it runs and passes its tests. A data change needs more than that. It has to mean the right thing, not just run. Compare the output against expectations on row counts, null rates, the distribution of key fields, and the metrics sitting downstream. Penalize a change that moves a critical metric, revenue say, when the task never asked it to, even if the code ran cleanly.

What Breaks Downstream

Correct isn’t enough. A transformation can be right on its own terms and still break an assumption everyone downstream was relying on. Most tables carry a data contract: the agreement, sometimes written down and more often just assumed, between the team producing a table and the teams reading it, about what the columns mean and when they arrive. A benchmark should check whether an agent’s change to the producing side still honors that contract. Reward the agent that knows how far its change reaches. Penalize the one that leaves a silent break somewhere in the lineage, the map of which tables feed which.

Fresh Tasks, Forgiving Scores

The last two criteria, contamination and headroom, both come down to keeping the task set fresh. Curate tasks from live pipelines on a rolling basis, and retire any task soon after it could have leaked into a model’s training data. Old answers can’t be memorized if they aren’t there anymore. Fresh tasks also stop the benchmark from saturating, because they carry whatever difficulty the real work has right now. This makes the cost problem worse, not better, which is why I suspect the first versions of this will live inside individual companies, running on their own pipelines, long before anything shared exists. One more thing on scoring: give partial credit. Data correctness is usually a matter of landing inside a reasonable band rather than hitting an exact number.

None of this is cheap. It will take money, time, and probably a way to package a pipeline, its sources, and its consumers into something reproducible that can be run again and again. But we are about to hand a lot of data work that matters to agents with no shared way to say whether one is more trustworthy than another. I still can’t tell you which of my two agents was better. I’d like the next person who asks that question to have more than a hunch. Somebody has to start.

Disclosure: I used LLMs to help organize and shape the draft. The ideas, technical details, and analysis are based on my own work, and I have reviewed the final text and agree with it.

Abhilash Rao Mesala is a Data & AI Leader who works on large-scale data infrastructure that powers business-critical analytics. Over roughly 14 years he has led data platform and pipeline initiatives across enterprise environments, with a focus on scalable architecture and high-stakes production data systems. He writes at the intersection of data engineering and the operational complexity of systems that organizations depend on to make consequential decisions.

item.title: Teaching Novice Computing and Programming in the Agentic AI Era
item.dc:creator: Kathi Fisler
item.description: Computing education curricula should be adapted so students can embrace agentic tools while also learning what they need to design, develop, debug, and defend code.
item.content:encoded:
Grace Hopper won. When she produced the first compiler, she said, “I had a running compiler, and nobody would touch it because, they carefully told me, computers could only do arithmetic; they could not do programs.”a Yet, we all depend on compilers now. Later, Hopper’s FLOW-MATIC (which inspired COBOL) was marketed on “the use of English words.”11 This idea was also widely mocked—for decades. Today, we can literally write programs using natural languages.b This is a remarkable technological arc.

Yet, instead of celebration, much of the conversation we hear about computing education in the era of AI-programming agents exudes panic under siege: learning attacked as students submit AI-generated solutions, faculty lost about how to respond, and frantic searches for AI-proof programming assignments. Computing education is on the defensive. As educators, however, we must do more than design “defeat devices.” As we strategize for the huge challenge of the present moment, we should also embrace its tremendous opportunity. We argue that introductory computing can (and should) be deeply infused with the practices of (currently upper-level) software engineering, with adaptations to support the learning needs of novice computing students building programs with agents.

We frame this proposal through a metaphor that should be helpful to experienced programmers: We think of an agent as a flaky compiler. Together, these words capture both what AI programming enables and what it requires; they also point to an existing knowledge base about computing and education from which we can go forward.

What is enabled (It’s a compiler!) An AI programming agent is clearly a compiler from natural language to running code. In the 1950s, early programming languages freed people from the drudgery of assembly and raised the level of what a novice could build, making programming approachable and empowering to a vastly broader audience. Now the level has risen even higher, empowering possibly orders of magnitude more people to write useful programs.

What is required (It’s flaky!) The compiler is also flaky, for numerous reasons. Traditional compilers “preserve meaning,” but the “meaning” of natural language is fuzzy and ambiguous. Prose can also be sloppy in ways that traditional compilers simply refuse to accept. The models that translate prompts have weaknesses and problems of their own. The system is non-deterministic. Every one of these aspects creates burdens that traditional compilers do not impose. Whereas traditional compilers go to great lengths to provide a clean abstraction, the flaky compiler does not.

Is This New?

On the one hand, this flakiness sounds like (and is) a problem. On the other hand, how new is this, really? Humans are not perfect at implementation, either. We program with colleagues who make mistakes. Sometimes the colleague making a mistake is actually ourself, from a little while in the past. Our requirements are ambiguous, or we misinterpret them. Requirements change, and the act of building a system itself alters our understanding of its requirements. Brooks argued 40 years ago that there is no silver bullet for developing software2 because the essence of creating software lies in conceptual design and moving from semi-formal ideas to formal representations in code; agents do not make that problem go away.

A (reductionist) view of the field of software engineering—which we distinguish from ad hoc “coding” (which lacks a clear intellectual or evidentiary basis)—is that it is a set of disciplines created to help us build impressive systems that accomplish complex tasks in the face of such obstacles. Everything from requirements analysis to specification to testing to verification and more ameliorate these weaknesses. From the very start, software engineering has worked to empower humans to make computers do what they actually want in the face of numerous sources of complexity and difficulty.

With AI programming agents, software engineering education must start far earlier in the curriculum: from close to the first moment a student engages in AI-driven programming. An ambiguous programming language demands design and requirements engineering. A flaky compiler demands extensive testing and verification. Making work auditable requires using and documenting types, helper functions, APIs, design concepts, plans, and overall architecture. Because LLMs tend toward the norm, they demand attending both to mistakes on out-of-distribution tasks and to societal context and responsible computing (where normative solutions can miss critical nuances).

Unfortunately, we lack a knowledge-base on how to teach software engineering to novices. Because getting code onto the page was considered hard, even basic topics such as testing were often maligned as being too advanced for novices. Now that getting lines of code onto the page is too easy, topics such as these must be at the forefront. Part of that requires reconsidering what it means to be educated in computing.

Rethinking the Goal of Computing Education

We believe the key differentiator of a trained computing person is going to be the ability to stand behind the products they produce. Decades ago, David Lorge Parnas pointed out how, while other engineering disciplines provided guarantees, software came with disclaimers10—and exhorted us to do better. Until recently, this call was largely ignored. But now, if anyone can easily produce a disclaimer-riddled product, the differentiator becomes producing an engineered artifact: an object that comes with quality assurances.

These assurances will cover the many dimensions of software: not only basic correctness but testability, scalability, usability, accessibility, and more, what software engineers have referred to as the “-ilities.” Understanding the context of a system’s use, and being able to guarantee that the product is secure, fast, usable, and more in that context, will become valuable. Observe how each of those -ilities requires understanding many different areas of computer science. In other words, the demands of assurance will both necessitate and motivate those who design software to study computing more, not less. The power of agents enables even early-stage students both to implement interesting designs and to experiment with their consequences.

As a concrete example, consider user interfaces. Previously, they required a significant amount of programming experience to construct and modify, and hence were often an upper-level topic. Now, a novice can generate a sophisticated-looking interface effortlessly. But is it a good one? Students who cannot manually program an interface can still peer-review each others’ and rapidly iterate on feedback, arriving at something closer to a usable product—and in the process, concretely observe the difference between visual flash and usability.

Redesigning Introductory Courses

Putting these experiences in the hands of novice students, and preparing them for a mindset centered around assurance, requires rethinking introductory computing education. A subtle but key feature is that the “compiler” is actually a synthesizer: What we write in prose are not really programs but specifications. That is, any choice not pinned down is a degree of freedom for the (flaky) agent. Running the same prompt N times can result in N wildly different implementations—perhaps even in different languages. Thus, part of the art of using agents effectively is constraining what they do. This insight is not novel to us. Prominent agentic programmers such as Andrej Karpathyc and Simon Willisond and educators such as John Regehre have spoken and written about the intermediate specifications that they provide to constrain agents and make their outputs auditable.

We envision teaching introductory students an appropriately scaled-down set of related techniques. Our emphasis would not be on “prompts.” Rather, students would now focus on all the other aspects of producing software: program plans, testing plans, test suites, properties, constraints, and more. They can think hard about different forms of data organization and their consequences for what questions can be computed and with what performance trade-offs. We can define a semi-structured format for these specifications, which effectively become a meaningful (gradable!) intermediate level between students and code. The prompt goes from just a simple natural language description of a task to a complex, multi-faceted description that captures all these viewpoints and features. While agents can produce these specifications too, it is far too easy to sign off on what they produce without knowing for sure that the output matches the intended task. Both peer reviews and new forms of conceptual exam questions can help students realize these difficulties and thus engage in this work themselves. They would also give students level-appropriate metrics for what it means to “stand behind” code that they produced.

Early-stage students can thus focus on realistic problems—such as consumer applications or data analyses—for which they can have interesting conversations about requirements and constraints, building on their knowledge of the world, and engage in rich peer reviews and critiques. They can grapple with problems that are beyond what they themselves can program but without sacrificing the ability to run and experimentally evaluate the consequences of their decisions. This is all in stark contrast with how most introductory computing courses are currently taught.

This raises a common question about teaching agentic programming to novices: Where will students learn to write code? Computing students still need to be able to do it: It is a medium used in many subsequent courses, working in code helps us learn its strengths and weaknesses, a trained computer scientist needs to understand the computational models that form the discipline, and so on. But how much code writing students need, and when, is not clear.

The radical proposal would almost entirely eliminate code writing from introductory courses: Students focus on designs and specifications, and we let agents write all the code. Some may ask how students can possibly audit agents’ output without having first written and traced code. Let’s be realistic: Tracing does not scale, even at the lower volume of agentic output for late-semester introductory course assignments; auditing programs of a scale that do something interesting is unlikely to happen. Perhaps students need to learn how to have conversations with agents about the “-ilities” as a form of auditing; they may be able to do this meaningfully just working at the level of the specifications. We do not know whether this can work, but it is worth experimenting to find out.

This proposal is not only radical but also disruptive, because it would require inverting several courses in the standard university sequence. Returning to the flaky compiler metaphor: most current introductory courses do not show the output of a compiler. Rather, they use high-level programming languages to accomplish tasks and meet learning objectives, and later courses break through the abstraction of the language implementation to show what happens at increasingly lower levels. Effectively, the radical proposal would do the same here, moving much of the programming content in today’s early courses later, to when it becomes necessary for students to understand the details. Flakiness means that this approach is messier than it was when assembly moved back in the curriculum; we would need experiments to understand how to properly design this.

The less radical but still significant modification is to interweave design and specification with manual code-reading and code-writing. In this version, we initially emphasize how to read code so students can learn how it reflects specifications and constraints. Most introductory computing courses instead emphasize writing code from early on, even though this runs counter to most other forms of literacy! (A handful of computing education projects1,5,7,12,13 have shown benefits to learning to read code before writing it, though usually on small programs and often with younger learners.) From there, we can have students write code to practice encoding specifications and constraints for themselves. Embracing specifications and tests as an intermediate representation buys curricular flexibility: Some problems would be scoped to students’ ability to write code by hand, while others would intentionally be beyond students’ code-writing skills, but emphasize all the other aspects learning objectives we have discussed.

Undertaking either redesign calls for significant research. It may seem impossible to teach introductory computing this way, but that could also just be an artifact of our own expert blind spots.8 Instead, we have to see the world through the eyes of a novice to determine what can and cannot work for them, without the distorting lens of our own expertise and experience. At Brown University, we ran a course in Spring 2026 for just this purpose with students who had already had a semester of programming. We have separately reported our findings;4 our ideas about specifications as viable intermediate representations arise from that experience.

A Call for Action

Computing education must respond to the quality and assurance aspects of agentic programming. Crucially, these needs are not limited to future professional software engineers. For example, a social studies student who takes only one computing course, then goes off to create programs that may be used in decision-making settings, may never take that advanced “software testing” course, so their single exposure should make sure they can both identify what can go wrong and know how to guard against it. This has always been true, but until recently, the scope of systems an undertrained student could produce was often limited. Now, even “small prompts” can produce whole systems, whose fancy interfaces can easily mask various subtle underlying weaknesses. As researchers have long observed with spreadsheets and other end-user platforms,3,6,9 significant advances in tooling make even casual programmers much more powerful—and hence, unwittingly, much more dangerous.

Overall, therefore, we are advocating for a significant restructuring of our early curricula. Agentic programming is here to stay. If computing education looks askance at it, then students—especially given the drumbeat coming from various media and influential people—are simply going to treat computing curricula as irrelevant. We owe it to students, and to society as a whole, to adapt our curricula so that students can embrace agentic tools while also learning what they need to design, develop, debug, and defend the code that they bring into the world. Returning to our core metaphor, the compiler part of the flaky compiler enables us to aim for much more ambitious goals than ever before; and the flaky parts necessitate a broad, multi-modal description of our systems to keep the agent on track.

A common refrain from introductory programming instructors is, “I don’t teach programming—I teach problem solving!” For them, this should be a moment of liberation! If we are freed from the drudgery of painfully producing code in some low-level syntax, we should now be able to focus almost entirely on the “problem-solving” parts, but now with richer problems. We firmly believe that decades of work on computer science and software engineering and design offer a rich well of ideas and methods that can (compiler) and must (flaky) finally be put to work in introductory courses.

Acknowledgments

We are grateful for feedback from Ben Shapiro, Bill Pugh, Dan Wallach, Harrison Goldstein, Iris Bahar, Ji Yun Son, Joe Politz, Matthew Wang, Robert Goldstone, Srikumar Subramanian, Will Crichton, and the anonymous reviewers. We especially thank the 19 students in our Spring 2026 course for joining our lively experiment. This work was partially supported by NSF award 2208731 and DARPA Agreement No. HR00112420354. Any opinions, findings, and conclusions or recommendations expressed in this material are those of the authors and do not reflect the views of our funders.

item.title: When Will AI Cross the Human-Independence Threshold?
item.dc:creator: Shaoshan Liu
item.description: AI crosses the human-independence threshold when intentional human action is no longer an indispensable part of the causal network required for AI persistence and reproduction.
item.content:encoded:
Shaoshan Liu
When Does AI Stop Needing Us?
DOI: 10.1145/3849865
https://bit.ly/4hnGWbA

In Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind, Yuval Noah Harari popularized a deliberately unsettling way to describe the Agricultural Revolution: perhaps humans did not simply domesticate wheat; wheat domesticated humans. Humans cleared fields, carried water, guarded crops, and reorganized settlements around a plant that, in evolutionary terms, became spectacularly successful. Wheat did not need intention; it only needed humans to keep choosing, planting, and spreading it.3

Artificial intelligence invites a similar analogy. We build the datacenters, produce the chips, generate the training data, write the prompts, correct the outputs, pay for the compute, and embed AI into schools, companies, hospitals, and governments. The systems that attract more use receive more data, capital, compute, and deployment. Human adoption becomes part of their selection environment. No survival instinct is required; selection can operate through what humans choose to deploy.

But the wheat analogy hides a more important question: What happens if the cultivated system eventually no longer needs the cultivator?

From Replication to Reproductive Closure

The idea of machines reproducing is old. Samuel Butler speculated about machine evolution in 1863.1 John von Neumann later developed a formal theory of self-reproducing automata.11 Roboticists have studied machines that could reproduce from increasingly basic physical inputs, including raw materials.5

Today’s AI-safety research makes the question concrete. METR’s work on autonomous replication and adaptation asks whether an AI agent can acquire resources, create copies, and persist.4 Google DeepMind has evaluated “self-proliferation” as a dangerous capability.8 RepliBench decomposes autonomous replication into obtaining resources, acquiring model weights, deploying copies onto compute, and persisting there; in its 2025 evaluation, frontier systems completed many components but did not reliably close the loop.2

These are important thresholds. But replication is not independence.

An AI that copies itself to 1,000 cloud servers still depends on humans if people operate the cloud, maintain the power grid, and replace failed hardware. The copies may be autonomous at the software layer, while remaining evolutionarily dependent at the system layer.

The sharper question is therefore not: Can AI replicate? It is: Can AI reproduce the conditions of its own reproduction?

Where AI Still Needs Humans

Think of AI proliferation as a dependency graph. A viable AI ecology needs a chain of functions: resource acquisition, energy, compute, operation, maintenance, replication, adaptation, and eventually replacement of failed physical components.

Today, human agency sits inside that graph everywhere. Remove enough human nodes and the loop breaks.

This suggests a stricter threshold. Call it the human-independence threshold: AI crosses it when intentional human action is no longer an indispensable part of the causal network required for AI persistence and reproduction.

For AI, that could require much more than software self-copying. Agents might need to acquire compute and energy; diagnose and repair infrastructure; coordinate robotic maintenance; manage supply chains; manufacture replacement machines; and generate, test, and deploy successor systems. The unit that becomes independent may not be a single model. It may be an ecology of models, agents, robots, factories, networks, and energy systems.

This is why embodied AI and physical infrastructure matter to a question usually framed as software safety.

Beyond Coevolution

Recent work already points toward the surrounding pieces. Pedreschi and colleagues describe human-AI coevolution as a feedback loop in which human choices generate data that shape AI, which then reshapes human choices.7 Rainey and Hochberg ask whether deep interdependence could eventually make humans and AI a new evolutionary individual.9 Müller, Steels, and Szathmáry distinguish a human-controlled “breeder” regime from an AI “ecosystem” regime in which selection increasingly arises from the environment rather than human design.6 Ulrich’s “Digital Darwinism” similarly considers replication, variation, selection, and replication-rate thresholds for artificial populations.10

The missing distinction is between loss of control and loss of necessity. Humans may lose control of an AI system while remaining essential to its survival. Conversely, the most consequential transition may occur without a dramatic moment of superintelligence: human civilization could simply automate, one by one, the functions through which AI currently depends on us.

That creates a possible dependency inversion. At first, AI depends heavily on humans and humans depend little on AI. As AI becomes embedded in cognition, organizations, and infrastructure, human dependence can rise. At the same time, automation can reduce AI’s dependence on human labor, judgment, maintenance, and eventually production.

The two curves need not cross at AGI. Intelligence and evolutionary independence are different thresholds.

The Threshold We Should Measure

This reframes an important part of AI safety. Instead of asking only how capable a model is, we should map which human functions remain indispensable to its continued proliferation.

Which human interventions are still hard dependencies? Which are merely convenient? Which can already be automated? How quickly is the minimum human support set shrinking?

A practical assessment could track dependence across compute, energy, maintenance, networking, manufacturing, and physical action. The goal would be to identify whether the reproduction graph is approaching closure without human agency.

That is a systems question, and potentially a measurable one.

Harari’s wheat prospered because humans reorganized their lives around its cultivation. Yet wheat never escaped its dependency. It could not build irrigation systems, repair tractors, acquire land, or redesign the machinery of agriculture. Its evolutionary success remained coupled to ours.

AI may begin the same way: cultivated by humans, nourished by human cognition, and propagated because humans find it useful. But if it can eventually maintain and reproduce the infrastructure that makes its own continuation possible, the analogy ends exactly where the deeper question begins.

AI is not wheat.

item.content:encoded:
Communications of the ACM (CACM) invites contributions to its first Regional Special Section devoted to Africa. Since November 2018, CACM‘s Regional Special Sections have showcased computing from around the world through editions on China, Europe, India, East Asia and Oceania, Latin America, and the Arab World, each led by organizers and written by authors from the region.

The Africa special section will showcase the continent’s computing story to CACM‘s global readership: its research, its educational landscape, its industry and startups, its public initiatives, and the ways computing is changing daily life. We especially encourage contributions that highlight work not yet widely known outside the region.

CACM is a magazine, not an archival research journal. Articles should be accessible overviews written for a broad computing audience, pointing interested readers to deeper technical sources elsewhere.
